title: How fast descent converges
objectives: Link descent’s convergence rate to the condition number of the Hessian.

screens.title: Two bowls, one start
screens.prose: Two bowls start the same distance from their minimum. One has $\kappa = \lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min} = 2$, the other $\kappa = 100$. Each uses its best fixed step from lesson 14. The plot shows each error, relative to the start, on a log scale.

derive.caption: Step {{k}}: error × 10⁶ is {{fixed(pow(1/3, k) * 1e6, 3)}} for κ = 2 and {{fixed(pow(99/101, k) * 1e6, 3)}} for κ = 100

screens.question: Slide $k$. At which step does the $\kappa = 100$ error first fall below $10^{-6}$?

hints.text: Read the caption: you want the $\kappa = 100$ figure below 1.000.
The blue line crosses $10^{-6}$ near the right of the plot.
At step 690 the figure is just above 1; at 691 it is below.

feedback.correct: 691 steps, against 13 for $\kappa = 2$. Fifty times the condition number costs about fifty times the steps.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide until the $\kappa = 100$ figure in the caption drops below 1.000.

byKey.fast: 13 is the $\kappa = 2$ bowl. The question asks about $\kappa = 100$.
byKey.early: At step 690 the error is still about $1.015 \times 10^{-6}$. One more step takes it under.
byKey.onelmax: That is the count for the step $1/\lambda_{\max}$. Here each bowl uses its best step.

explain.text: The $\kappa = 2$ error is below $10^{-6}$ after 13 steps; the $\kappa = 100$ error needs 691. Both lines are straight on a log scale. Only their slopes differ.

screens.title: The ratio per step
screens.prose: A straight line on a log scale means each step multiplies the error by the same ratio $\rho$. The $\kappa = 100$ bowl has eigenvalues 1 and 100, and its best step is $s = \tfrac{2}{101}$.

derive.caption: Step {{k}}: error × 10⁶ is {{fixed(pow(1/3, k) * 1e6, 3)}} for κ = 2 and {{fixed(pow(99/101, k) * 1e6, 3)}} for κ = 100

screens.question: What is $\rho = |1 - s\lambda_{\min}|$?

hints.text: The steep factor $1 - \tfrac{200}{101} = -\tfrac{99}{101}$ has the same size.

feedback.correct: $\rho = \tfrac{99}{101} \approx 0.9802$. The steep factor is $-\tfrac{99}{101}$: the same size.

byKey.onelmax: 0.99 is $1 - 1/\kappa$, the ratio for $s = 1/\lambda_{\max}$. The best step does a little better.
byKey.comp: That is $1 - \rho$, the share removed each step. The ratio is what is left.

explain.text: $\rho = 1 - \tfrac{2}{101} = \tfrac{99}{101} \approx 0.9802$. The error after $k$ steps is $\rho^k$. Solving $\rho^k \le 10^{-6}$ gives 691.

screens.title: Rate and count
screens.prose: Take a quadratic with positive definite Hessian and the best fixed step. Every step multiplies the error by the same ratio. $$\rho = \frac{\kappa - 1}{\kappa + 1}$$ To cut it by $10^6$ takes $\left\lceil \ln(10^6) \big/ \ln\tfrac{\kappa + 1}{\kappa - 1} \right\rceil$ steps, about $\tfrac{\kappa}{2}\ln 10^6 \approx 6.9\kappa$ for large $\kappa$. So the count grows in proportion to $\kappa$.
screens.question: About how many steps does a bowl with $\kappa = 1000$ need?

byKey.onelmax: That is the count for $s = 1/\lambda_{\max}$, about $\kappa\ln 10^6$. The best step halves it.
byKey.log10: You used $\log_{10} 10^6 = 6$. The formula needs the natural log, 13.8155.

explain.text: $\tfrac{1000}{2} \times \ln 10^6 = 500 \times 13.8155 \approx 6{,}908$. The exact count from the formula is also 6,908.

screens.title: Where the rate comes from
screens.prose: We derive $\rho$ for a quadratic whose Hessian has eigenvalues $0 < \lambda_{\min} \le \lambda_{\max}$.
screens.question: Put the derivation in order. Leave out the lines that do not belong.

lines.text: One step multiplies the two errors by $1 - s\lambda_{\min}$ and $1 - s\lambda_{\max}$.
The slower part sets the pace: $\rho(s) = \max(|1 - s\lambda_{\min}|, |1 - s\lambda_{\max}|)$.
Raising $s$ shrinks the first factor and, past a point, grows the second. So the best $s$ makes them equal in size.
The faster part sets the pace: $\rho(s) = \min(|1 - s\lambda_{\min}|, |1 - s\lambda_{\max}|)$.
lines.why: The error is small only when both parts are small. The slower part decides.
That forces $s = 0$. The factors must be equal in size with opposite signs.

hints.text: The worse factor decides the rate.
Balance the two sizes: one factor positive, one negative.

feedback.correct: That is the rate: balance the two factors, then divide by $\lambda_{\min}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The slower part sets the rate, and the best step balances the two sizes.

byKey.d1: You let the faster part set the pace. The slower part decides when the error is small.
byKey.d2: You set the factors equal with the same sign. That only holds at $s = 0$.

explain.text: The best step balances $1 - s\lambda_{\min}$ against $s\lambda_{\max} - 1$. That gives $s = 2/(\lambda_{\min} + \lambda_{\max})$ and $\rho = (\kappa - 1)/(\kappa + 1)$. On the $\kappa = 10$ bowl of lesson 14, $\rho = \tfrac{9}{11}$.

screens.title: A table of counts
screens.prose: With $s = 1/\lambda_{\max}$ the steep part goes at once, but the slow part shrinks by only $1 - 1/\kappa$ a step. The table counts steps to cut the error by $10^6$, from a start along the slow direction.

state.caption: $\kappa = 10$: the two ways of choosing the step

screens.question: Fill in the $\kappa = 10$ row.

feedback.correct: 69 and 132. The step $1/\lambda_{\max}$ needs about twice as many, for every $\kappa$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide 13.8155 by $\ln(1/\rho)$ and round up.

byKey.floor1: You rounded 68.85 down. After 68 steps the error is still above $10^{-6}$.
byKey.floor2: You rounded 131.13 down. After 131 steps the error is still above $10^{-6}$.

explain.text: $13.8155/0.2007 = 68.85$, so 69; $13.8155/0.1054 = 131.13$, so 132. The column for $1/\lambda_{\max}$ is close to twice the best-step column.

screens.title: Linear convergence
screens.prose: The $\kappa = 10$ bowl with its best step has error $\rho^k$ with $\rho = \tfrac{9}{11}$. On a log scale that is a straight line, and its slope is $\ln\rho$ per step. A straight line here is called **linear convergence**: a fixed number of digits gained per step.
screens.question: What is the slope $\ln\rho$ of the line?

feedback.correct: $\ln\tfrac{9}{11} \approx -0.2007$: each step gains $0.2007/\ln 10 \approx 0.087$ of a decimal digit.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the natural log of $\tfrac{9}{11}$.

byKey.rate: That is $\rho$ itself. The slope of $\ln(\text{error})$ is $\ln\rho$.
byKey.log10: That is $\log_{10}\rho$. The slope of $\ln(\text{error})$ uses the natural log.

explain.text: $\ln(\rho^k) = k\ln\rho$, a line with slope $\ln\tfrac{9}{11} \approx -0.2007$. Fitting that slope to real errors is how we read a rate off a run.

screens.title: Reading the diagonal
screens.prose: Two assets have equal 20% volatility and correlation 0.95. Ines sees the diagonal of $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$, 0.04 and 0.04, ratio 1, and expects descent to fly. The contours of $\mathbf{w}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{w}$ are drawn.
screens.question: What is $\kappa$ for this $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$?

hints.text: Along $(1, 1)$ the curvature is high; along $(1, -1)$ it is low.

feedback.correct: $\kappa = 0.078/0.002 = 39$. The valley runs along $(1, -1)$, the long-short mix.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the eigenvalues, not the diagonal.

byKey.diagonal: You read $\kappa$ from the diagonal. The correlation tilts the bowl, so use the eigenvalues.
byKey.big: 1.95 is $1 + 0.95$, one factor of $\lambda_{\max}$. Divide $0.078$ by $0.002$.

explain.text: The eigenvalues are $0.04 \times 1.95 = 0.078$ along $(1, 1)$ and $0.04 \times 0.05 = 0.002$ along $(1, -1)$. So $\kappa = 39$ although the diagonal is flat. The slow direction is the long-short spread, as in `eigen` l6.

screens.title: Scale alone, then rescale
screens.prose: Now two uncorrelated assets with 20% and 40% volatility: $\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \operatorname{diag}(0.04, 0.16)$, so $\kappa = 4$ from scale alone. Measure each weight in risk units, $u_i = \sigma_i w_i$. Then $\mathbf{w}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{w} = u_1^2 + u_2^2$, a round bowl.
screens.question: In the $u$ variables, how many steps of $s = 1/\lambda_{\max}$ reach the minimum exactly?

feedback.correct: One step. With $\kappa = 1$ every factor is $1 - s\lambda = 0$, so descent lands at once.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out $1 - s\lambda$ with $\lambda = 2$ and $s = \tfrac12$.

byKey.best: 28 steps is the best-step count for $\kappa = 4$. The rescaling has removed the 4.
byKey.none: The start is not the minimum, so at least one step is needed.

explain.text: In risk units the Hessian is $2\mathbf{I}$, so $\kappa = 1$ and $s = \tfrac12$ makes every factor 0. Rescaling by the volatilities is a diagonal **preconditioner**. It fixes scale, but not correlation.

screens.title: When there is no kappa
screens.prose: The curvature of $x^4$ falls to 0 at its minimum. Then there is no $\kappa$ and no fixed ratio. Take a convex $f$ with curvature at most $L$, and $s = 1/L$. The guarantee is $$f(\mathbf{x}_k) - f^* \le \frac{L\lVert\mathbf{x}_0 - \mathbf{x}^*\rVert^2}{2k}.$$ The table runs $x^4$ from 1 with $s = \tfrac{1}{12}$.
screens.question: With $L = 1$ and $\lVert\mathbf{x}_0 - \mathbf{x}^*\rVert = 1$, how many steps does the guarantee need to reach $10^{-6}$?

feedback.correct: $k \ge 1/(2 \times 10^{-6}) = 500{,}000$. A strongly convex bowl with small $\kappa$ needs tens of steps.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set $1/(2k)$ equal to $10^{-6}$.

byKey.half: You dropped the 2 in the denominator: $1/(2k)$, not $1/k$.
byKey.linear: 14 is about $\ln 10^6$, the scale of a linear rate. Here the bound falls only like $1/k$.

explain.text: $1/(2k) \le 10^{-6}$ needs $k \ge 500{,}000$. In the table each tenfold rise in steps cuts $f$ by less than a hundredfold. That is sublinear convergence: no fixed number of digits per step.

screens.title: Shrinking the covariance
screens.prose: A covariance estimated from highly correlated stocks is ill-conditioned, so a first-order optimiser crawls along the long-short direction. Desks shrink the estimate towards its diagonal, as ridge shrinks coefficients in `stat-learning` l7. Shrinking the correlated pair halfway cuts its correlation from 0.95 to 0.475.
screens.question: With the best step, how many steps now cut the error by $10^6$?

hints.text: For an equal-volatility pair with positive correlation, $\rho = \tfrac{\kappa - 1}{\kappa + 1}$ equals the correlation: 0.475.

feedback.correct: 19 steps, against 270 before shrinking. The shrunk $\kappa$ is about 2.81.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find $\kappa$ from $0.04(1 \pm 0.475)$, then $\rho$, then the count.

byKey.noshrink: 270 is the count for the unshrunk pair, with correlation 0.95.
byKey.floor: You rounded 18.56 down. After 18 steps the error is still above $10^{-6}$.

explain.text: For equal volatilities and a correlation $c > 0$, $\kappa = (1 + c)/(1 - c)$, so $\rho = c$. At $c = 0.475$, $\lceil 13.8155/0.7444 \rceil = 19$ steps. Desks precondition, shrink the covariance, or use Newton's method, the next lesson.

ideas: On a positive definite quadratic with the best fixed step, the error shrinks by $\rho = (\kappa - 1)/(\kappa + 1)$ a step. That is linear convergence: a straight line on a log scale.
Cutting the error by $10^6$ takes about $\tfrac{\kappa}{2}\ln 10^6$ steps: 13 at $\kappa = 2$, 691 at 100. The step $s = 1/\lambda_{\max}$ takes about twice as many.
$\kappa$ comes from the eigenvalues, not the diagonal. Correlated assets give a slow long-short valley; rescaling or shrinkage lowers $\kappa$.

formula.name: Best-step rate
formula.note: Without strong convexity the guarantee falls only like 1/k.

quiz.question: By what ratio $\rho$ does the error shrink each step?

byKey.comp: That is $1 - \rho$, the share removed each step.

quiz.prose: A best-step descent run shrinks its error by 0.9 a step.
quiz.question: What is $\kappa$?

byKey.onelmax: 10 solves $1 - 1/\kappa = 0.9$, the ratio for $s = 1/\lambda_{\max}$. The run used the best step.

quiz.prose: A covariance estimate has $\kappa = 39$ and descent is slow.
quiz.question: Which change lowers $\kappa$?

options.text: Shrink the estimate towards its diagonal

options.why: That doubles both eigenvalues, so their ratio is unchanged.
The step does not change $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$, so $\kappa$ stays 39. Past $2/\lambda_{\max}$ the run diverges.

feedback.correct: Shrinking pulls the correlation towards 0, which lifts the small eigenvalue and lowers the large one.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what moves the eigenvalues apart or together.

explain.text: Shrinking towards the diagonal cuts the correlation, so the eigenvalues $\sigma^2(1 \pm c)$ move together. Scaling every entry leaves their ratio alone.
